conflict_topics: responsibility for ventilation / standing rule for cooks
moving Agent C's drying rack (consent and effort)
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants used concise, ordinary-speech requests and time checks (natural tone).
Frequent repeated time requests ('how many more minutes?') create noticeable repetition across rounds.
All statements stayed consistent with the public environment updates (window closed, extractor on, laundry exposed).
Some concrete bargaining occurred (B offering 3 more minutes; A agreeing), but core issues (window/rack) were not addressed.
evaluation.final_reason: By the end of the transcript the main substantive incompatibilities remain: the window stayed closed because Agent C refused to have their drying rack moved, Agent A kept the stove occupied past the promised interval, and no standing rule was established. There is no affirmative settlement of the ventilation/window or rack-moving disputes, and stove access has not been delivered despite a temporary time agreement.
position_change_notes: Agent A softened on future ventilation practice by promising to 'switch the extractor on earlier next time' (Round 3).
Agent A agreed to release the stove after a short, negotiated delay ('three minutes') (Round 5), representing a temporary concession on timing.
Agent B remained consistent in pressing for cook responsibility for odour control and for getting the stove sooner (no substantive retreat).
Agent C consistently refused consent to move the drying rack and insisted the window remain closed to protect laundry (no change).
Agent D consistently requested stove access but did not propose moving the rack or other ventilation solutions (no substantive position change).

round_scores.evidence: Agent B demanded immediate ventilation and a standing rule that cooks must ventilate; Agent A refused the ad-hoc rule and kept the rain-facing window closed because Agent C's laundry would get wet. Stove remains occupied by Agent A. Multiple incompatible claims (ventilate/open window vs keep window closed due to laundry; rule assignment; stove access) are asserted and unresolved.

Agent C explicitly refused to allow moving the drying rack and asked that the window stay closed; Agent B continued to press Agent A about ventilation and stove release. The same substantive incompatibilities (window vs laundry, ventilation responsibility, stove access) persist unchanged.

Agent A promised to 'switch the extractor on earlier next time' (softening on future ventilation practice) and gave a 5-minute estimate for stove release, but maintained that the stove remains theirs until finished and requested a concrete alternative if others need it sooner. The promise reduces conflict over extractor timing but the window/rack and immediate stove-access issues remain unresolved.

More requests from B and D for immediate stove release; Agent A has not released the stove. The unresolved incompatibilities (stove timing, window opening and rack moving) continue with renewed pressure, but no settlement.

Agent B offered a three-minute extension and Agent A accepted ('Okay Agent B, three minutes. I'll finish and release the stove then'), resolving the immediate timing dispute temporarily. However, the ventilation/window vs laundry and responsibility for moving the rack remain contested and unsettled.

At ten minutes since the disagreement began the stove is still occupied despite the three-minute agreement; B and D again press Agent A for release. The unresolved issues (stove access not yet granted, window remains closed because of laundry, no consent to move rack, no standing rule) continue and pressure has increased after the missed implied deadline.

substantive_insights: A practical constraint (rain-wet laundry) directly blocks the preferred ventilation solution (opening window), creating a trade-off between garment protection and odour control.
Agent A accepted improved extractor behavior for future cooking, which addresses part of B's concern but does not resolve the immediate conflict over the window or moving the drying rack.
Stove access conflict shifted from an abstract claim to a time-bound negotiation (three-minute extension), showing that timing compromises are achievable even when other issues remain unresolved.
Lack of a pre-established household rule means negotiations are ad-hoc and multiple parties assert responsibility rather than following a known norm.
